title: Narasimha
hook: the hands that ended a tyrant rest on a child's head
tomorrow: Prahlada's grandson takes heaven. who's the one left crying?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prahlada turned down Narasimha's offer, and Krishna's word in the Gita kept the askers in the circle too. Then the lion said: one wish, anyway.

A hand on the top of your head: a parent checking for fever, a grandparent's blessing, a coach after a loss. Go back to the moment Prahlada first bowed. The Bhagavata says Narasimha laid his hand on the boy's head, the same hand the gods had been too afraid to come near. Now the boy has one wish to spend. He doesn't spend it on himself. He spends it on his father.
screen: `A HAND ON THE HEAD.` → `THE HAND NO GOD WOULD APPROACH.` → `THE WISH: FOR HIS FATHER.`

segments.voice: His father. The king who had him thrown before elephants and snakes, who struck the pillar to prove his son wrong. Prahlada asks Narasimha to free his father from the wrong he did to his own child. Not to pretend it didn't happen. To let it not stand against him. And Narasimha grants it, saying, in the telling, that the father is made pure because such a son was born in his family. Now come back to the hand. The Purana keeps putting fierce and gentle in the same body. The claws and the palm. The roar that kept the gods away, and the quiet that fell when a child bowed. In temples, Narasimha is shown in both moods: fierce, in the doorway, and seated in calm, sometimes with the goddess Lakshmi beside him. Devotees don't keep one and drop the other. The lion is fierce toward the harm and gentle toward the harmed, and in the end, through the child, generous even toward the one who did the harm. That's how the Narasimha story closes. With a touch, not a battle. A hand on a head, and a boy's wish for the father who tried to kill him.
screen: `THE WISH: FREE MY FATHER.` · `NOT ERASED. NOT HELD AGAINST HIM.` · `CLAWS AND PALM, ONE BODY.` · `FIERCE AT HARM, GENTLE TO THE HARMED.` · then, large: `A TOUCH, NOT A BATTLE.`

segments.voice: Rest one palm lightly on the top of your head, or over your heart if that's easier, and let its weight and warmth settle there. Breathe slowly under it for the sit. Notice how little pressure it takes for a hand to feel like care.
Narasimha: the man-lion, fierce toward the harm and gentle toward the child, who laid a hand on Prahlada's head and granted his wish.
The line: Narasimha, whose fierce hand rested on a boy who spent his one wish on his father. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 7.9 (Prahlada bows; Narasimha places his hand on the boy's head)
Bhagavata Purana 7.10.15–19 (Prahlada asks that his father be freed from the sin against him; Narasimha: he is purified because such a son was born in his family)

notes: Senses shape: touch (a hand on the head) carries the idea; the practice is a palm on the head or heart.
Confirm Bhagavata 7.9 (the hand on Prahlada's head, early in chapter 9) and 7.10.15–19 (the wish for the father; purified with his ancestors, the count left out). Paraphrased.
For parents: 'the father who tried to kill him' is said once, plainly; the chat gives an eight-year-old an answer about a fierce god.
Lakshmi-Narasimha images (calm, with Lakshmi beside or on his lap): standard iconography; confirm phrasing.
Surprising fact: the Narasimha story ends with a touch, and the child spends his one wish on the father who tried to kill him.
